schools.summary: Gill dates the marriage three years after Sarah's death, when Abraham was a hundred and forty, but reports a bishop's opinion that answers the objection: that Abraham took Keturah as a concubine some twenty years after marrying Sarah, when she proved barren and long before Hagar, the notice being deferred so as not to break the thread of the history; he supports it from her being called a concubine and from Abraham's having great-grandchildren by her. Calvin calls the late dating very absurd, since Abraham was dead in his own body thirty-eight years before Sarah died and Paul commends his faith on that ground, so it would be unworthy of the man's gravity that one cold and impotent at a hundred should father many sons forty years afterwards.

Henry takes the plain order of the narrative: Abraham had buried Sarah and married off Isaac, the two dear companions of his life, and being now solitary with his household wanting a governess he took Keturah, probably the chief of his maidservants, marriage not being forbidden to old age. He looks past the names of the six sons to the promise, seeing in so late a family a part-fulfilment of what was said about the increase of Abraham's posterity.

Wesley follows Henry on the marriage and presses the point about the sons further, that the strength Abraham received by the promise still remained in him, to show how far the virtue of a promise exceeds the power of nature. Clarke is readier than the rest to hunt the names in the map, offering a city named from Zimran on the authority of Stephanus Byzantinus while thinking it likelier, with Calmet, that all these sons lived in Arabia Deserta; he reports that several learned men identify Jokshan with the father of the Arabs, gives Medan and Midian to the country east of the Dead Sea, and derives the brook Jabbok from Ishbak and the Sacceans from Shuah.

Ellicott holds the date undecided, since the Hebrew says only that Abraham added and took a wife; it is possible Isaac's marriage left him solitary and he took Keturah then, the sole objection being his own words that a son was beyond nature for a man of a hundred. He thinks the supposed traces of the six names in Arabia untrustworthy, though Josephus and Jerome place the family in Arabia Felix, and singles out the one name with a future: Midian's race became famous traders, and since the same men are called Medanites in one verse and Midianites in another the two tribes probably coalesced, Jethro belonging to them. Keil and Delitzsch work the second generation the same way, connecting Sheba with the Sabaeans who stole Job's oxen and Dedan with the traders named beside Tema.

sides.position: after Sarah’s death, in the order the narrative gives — he was solitary and his household wanted a governess
during Sarah’s lifetime — Abraham was dead in his own body thirty-eight years before she died, and Paul says so
undecided — the Hebrew says only that Abraham added and took a wife

the sons of Keturah and the tribes of Arabia

3.pericope_label: The sons of the concubines sent away

schools.summary: Gill takes the gift of all to Isaac as a last will rather than a delivery in Abraham's lifetime, since he plainly reserved something for himself and for gifts to the others, so the words may be rendered had given; and he explains what a concubine was in this household, a half wife or secondary one, espoused but not by writing, ranking as a head servant, whose children did not inherit. Calvin faces how the dismissal appears: to constitute one son sole heir and send the rest away with gifts was apparently harsh and cruel, but it was agreeable to God's appointment, and Abraham was not at liberty to divide at his own pleasure an inheritance granted entire to another. He is careful that nobody take it for a precedent, since a man who now disinherited his other sons would do them injury and light a flame of pernicious strife in his family.

Clarke reckons the estate as the principal flocks and above all the right to Canaan, guesses the gifts to have been cattle for breeding, seed and implements of husbandry, and explains the sending away as a precaution taken while Abraham lived, lest after his death the others dispute a settlement in the land of promise with Isaac. From that circumstance, he says, arose the law prevailing in almost every country by which the estate goes to the eldest son of a lawful wife, and he adds a parallel from Solon, whose law excluded natural children from the paternal inheritance while allowing a present not exceeding a thousand drachmas. Wesley makes the gift to Isaac a matter of justice rather than favour, owed to Sarah his first wife and to Rebekah, who had married him on the assurance of it.

Ellicott extends the dispersion to Arabia and southern Mesopotamia, where by their superior vigour and organisation the descendants of Abraham established their supremacy over the natives, and closes with an observation from Burckhardt that the Bedaween still follow the practice, each younger son being given his share and moving off, leaving the eldest brother in quiet possession of the home. Keil and Delitzsch take up the phrase that will describe Abraham's own end: to be gathered to his people is constantly distinguished from dying and from being buried, and means reunion in Sheol with friends already gone, so the expression presupposes a belief in the personal continuance of a man after death, which the promises of God had raised in the patriarchs from a presentiment into a firm assurance of faith.

outliers.claim: insists the dismissal must not be taken as a precedent — Abraham was compelled by the grant made to Isaac, and a father who now singled out one heir would light a flame of pernicious strife

themes: Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac
unto the sons of the concubines he gave gifts
gathered to his people, and what the phrase presupposes
the eldest son and the law of inheritance

schools.summary: Calvin counts the hundred and seventy-five years as a pilgrimage and praises a wonderful and incomparable patience, Abraham having wandered a hundred years while God led him about, content in life and death with the bare promise; let those be ashamed who find it hard to bear the disquiet of a year or two. On the closing phrase he quarrels with an inference: those are mistaken who take gave up the ghost for a sudden and painless death, since Moses means the father of the faithful was not exempt from the common lot, so our minds should not languish when the outward man perishes but let this frail tabernacle be dissolved with tranquillity. Gill takes the very reading Calvin rejects, having Abraham go readily and cheerfully, with no previous sickness and no pain, by mere decay of nature.
Henry marks the transfer of the blessing as the point of the passage, that the blessing of Abraham did not die with him but survived to all the children of the promise.

Clarke thinks the phrase the days of the years has a beauty too little regarded, since good men do not live by centuries nor even count by years but by days, as creatures of a day spending it with reference to eternity. He dissents from the English rendering gave up the ghost, the Hebrew verb signifying to pant for breath and cease breathing, so that expired would everywhere be proper; ghost now means only the immortal spirit, and giving up a spirit is no act proper to man. He is less sanguine about the heir than the others, asking how little we hear in Isaac of the work of faith and the patience of hope, and observing that only one Abraham ever appeared where there should have been many imitators. Wesley finds in the good old age both a discharge and a crown, adds that a good man dies full of days even if he does not die old, and distinguishes the two gatherings, the body to the congregation of the dead and the soul to the congregation of the blessed.

Ellicott works the arithmetic out to a domestic result: Abraham was seventy-five when he left Haran, so his sojourn in Canaan lasted a hundred years, a quarter of it spent in the trial of his faith before Isaac was given; and since the twins were born when Isaac was sixty, they were fifteen when their grandfather died and had probably often seen him. Keil and Delitzsch notice who buried him, Isaac and Ishmael together, since Ishmael, though shut out from the covenant, had been acknowledged by God as Abraham's son in a distinct blessing and so stood above Keturah's sons; they add that the blessing passed to Isaac, who settled by Hagar's well, having been there already.

debates.question: What does gave up the ghost imply about how Abraham died?

those who read it so are mistaken — Moses means he was not exempt from the common lot
the English is at fault altogether — the verb means to cease breathing, and expired is the proper word

schools.summary: Gill puts the purpose of the list shortly, that the Lord was not unmindful of what he had said about multiplying Abraham's seed. Calvin values the fulfilment as evidence of God's veracity and thinks it no common gift that Ishmael should have twelve sons holding rank over as many tribes; but he is careful to call the benefit adventitious, superadded to the spiritual covenant, and observes that once the towns are enumerated Moses buries the whole race in oblivion, so that a substantial perpetuity remains only in the Church.

Clarke sees the writer showing how the promises were fulfilled to both branches, Isaac's blessing having just been noticed and Ishmael's increase now proved. On the towns and castles he takes the first for places of encampment in the wilderness, such as the Arabs have used from the remotest times, and the second for towers, probably mountain tops, fortified rocks and fastnesses in wooded or hilly country. Wesley marks the close of the line rather than its spread, taking Ishmael's hundred and thirty-seven years as recorded to show the efficacy of Abraham's prayer that Ishmael might live before God, and noting that he too was gathered to his people and died in the presence of all his brethren, with his friends about him, a thing anyone might wish for.

Ellicott states the rule the book follows, that Ishmael is not dismissed without a short record, after which he falls into the background and the historian returns to his main subject, the preparation of the race of whom Christ came; and he gives a reason for keeping such notices at all, that it was God's purpose the Jewish Messiah should be the Redeemer of the Gentiles too. Against Clarke he denies there were any towns or castles in the wilderness of Paran, defining the first word as an unwalled but settled village and the second, rendered castle here and tent in the Psalms, as a cluster of tents, the movable encampment of a tribe; from the distinction he draws an ethnography of two classes of Arabs, the nomads and the agricultural sort, who are reckoned inferiors and to this day pay a kind of blackmail to the nobler tribes. Keil and Delitzsch note that by the settled plan of Genesis this account precedes the history of Isaac, connect Nebajoth and Kedar with the rich flock-owners of Isaiah and, on the current opinion which Wetzstein disputes, with Pliny's Nabataeans.

19.pericope_label: Isaac entreats the Lord for Rebekah

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin mark the turn of the narrative, what was said of the Ishmaelites having been incidental, so that Moses takes up the subject he is really concerned with, which Calvin calls the progress of the Church. Calvin then presses the delay hardest of any: nothing seems less accordant with reason than that the propagation of the Church should be so small and so slow, Abraham in extreme old age receiving a slender solace with all his hope centred in one man, and Isaac himself bordering on old age and still not a father; who would not suppose God was dealing deceitfully in leaving those houses empty? He answers that the twenty years were meant so, that despair might give the greater lustre to a blessing suddenly granted. On the prayer he takes the recourse itself as evidence of two things Isaac knew, that he was childless because God had not blessed him and that fruitfulness is a special gift, distributed in various degrees to show men are not born fortuitously; and he adds that though Moses says in a single word that Isaac obtained offspring by prayer, reason dictates the praying had gone on for years. Gill notes that the word implies earnest and constant supplication, and reports the alternative rendering before his wife, she being present and joining in it.

Henry finds the arrangement of the chapter odd, since the entrance of these twins into the world is unusually the most considerable part of their story, little being told of Isaac himself except what bears on his father while he lived and on his sons afterwards; Isaac, he thinks, was no man of action nor much tried, but spent his days in quietness and silence. He counts the barrenness at twenty years and draws the lesson that though the accomplishment of God's promise is always sure it is often slow and seems crossed by Providence, so that faith may be tried and mercies long waited for be the more welcome. He notices too what Isaac did not do while the mercy was delayed: he did not approach a handmaid's bed, as Abraham had done and Jacob would, for he loved Rebekah.

Clarke notes that a new section of the law begins here, makes the childless years nineteen rather than twenty, and thinks the form of the original worth notice, since Isaac entreated the Lord directly and purposely for his wife; he cites Ainsworth for their praying together and the rabbins for the tradition that the two went to Mount Moriah, where Isaac had once been bound, and prayed there for a son. He sees a pattern besides, God exercising Isaac's faith before Jacob's birth as he had Abraham's before Isaac's. Wesley states the principle, that God's promises must not supersede our prayers but encourage them, and that Isaac, having prayed many years unheard, did not leave off.

Keil and Delitzsch give the reason for the delay in a sentence: the seed of the promise had to be prayed for from the Lord, so that it might not be taken merely for a fruit of nature but received and recognised as a gift of grace.

22.pericope_label: The children struggle, and the oracle

schools.summary: Gill calls the motion in the womb extraordinary, the two striving as if for mastery, and takes it for an emblem of the difference between Esau and Jacob, of the contentions of their offspring, and of the conflict between flesh and spirit in good men. Calvin rejects outright the reading that makes Rebekah's cry a woman's impatience: the complaint was extorted not by pain but by abhorrence of a prodigy, since she saw the conflict had no natural cause but portended a dreadful end, and felt the fear of divine anger stealing over her, as the faithful trace an evil to its source and tremble at the apprehension of judgment. He grants she was at first more disturbed than she should have been, but she soon found a remedy, and by her example we learn not to indulge sorrow excessively in perplexing affairs.

Clarke translates the verb as dashing against or bruising each other, so violent that the mother feared for her own safety and her children's, and reads her broken words as meaning, if I must suffer such things, why did I ever wish for a child — a speech not uncommon, he says, in a first pregnancy. On the enquiry he canvasses Melchizedek, Shem and Abraham, ruling out Shem as ten years dead while allowing that Abraham was living, and adds the wry remark that she went to enquire of the Lord as women now consult a physician, intercourse with God being less common than in those times of primitive simplicity. He quotes Bishop Newton for the principle governing the whole oracle, that these prophecies were meant not so much of single persons as of whole nations, since what was predicted of the brothers was verified in their posterity. Wesley mentions Melchizedek as the possible oracle, or some Urim or Teraphim, and turns the uncertainty to use, the word and prayer by which we now enquire giving great relief to the perplexed.

Keil and Delitzsch hear something graver in the cry than impatience, an evil omen that the pregnancy so long entreated would end in misfortune and the fruit of her womb miss the promised blessing, so that she asks in intense excitement wherefore am I alive; they report the guesses about how she enquired and observe that consulting a prophet was frequent in later Israel but improbable in the patriarchal age. Ellicott refuses the conjectures altogether: God spoke directly, as of old to Adam and Eve, and we read of no appearance and must not invent one, since the manner has not been revealed and it is enough to know that Jehovah did speak to men. He takes the answer as poetry in four lines and reads them in order, the second showing that even in childhood the sons would be unlike and unfriendly, then their growth into hostile nations, and last the prediction that the son who began with the birthright and the greater force of arms would end in the inferior place; he names a secondary cause, Jacob's people being settled by Joseph in the fruitful Delta and constantly reinforced by Semitic immigrants.

not female impatience but abhorrence of a prodigy and fear of divine anger
an evil omen that the long-entreated pregnancy would miss the promised blessing

24.pericope_label: The birth of the twins and the divided house

schools.summary: Gill records that Esau's red was either his body or the hair covering it, and passes on Jarchi's reading that it foretold a shedder of blood, as he and his posterity proved; on the parents' preference he explains Isaac's taste literally, the venison being in his mouth, that is, to his liking. Calvin reads the word used of Jacob antithetically rather than as praise, Moses setting the mild disposition of a man who loved home so much that he might seem indolent against the vigour of a brother addicted to hunting. He turns the partiality itself into evidence: God let Esau be so preferred in his father's affection that Jacob looked a rejected man, precisely to show that his election needs no assistance and can overcome any obstacle, so that it is intolerable presumption to make that adoption depend on the will of man.

Henry has Esau hunt with such dexterity that he became a conqueror ruling his neighbours, while Jacob liked the true delights of retirement better than all pretended pleasures, a stranger and pilgrim in spirit and a shepherd all his days. On the divided affections he warns that godly parents may feel their affections drawn to a godly child yet must not show partiality, lest evils arise.

Clarke takes the redness for red hair all over, confirmed later when Rebekah had to use kid-skins on Jacob's hands and neck, and is uncertain about the name Esau, since the root may mean made or perfected while the Arabic gives to make firm; he guesses the child was so called for seeming more robust than his brother. On the second name he derives it from a verb meaning to defraud, that is, to overthrow a man by tripping his heels, and takes the grasp as emblematic of Jacob's supplanting his brother. Wesley says Esau was red and hairy as though already grown, an indication of a strong constitution, while Jacob was smooth and tender as other children; he reads the name the same way Clarke does, as signifying both the pursuit of the birthright from the first and the eventual prevailing for it, and allows both senses of the word describing Jacob, an honest man who dealt fairly and one who kept to the tents either as shepherd or as a student.

Ellicott makes the redness a secondary reason for the later name Edom, notes that the words describing the down are elsewhere used of the sheepskin jacket worn by prophets, and takes the covering for a sign of a vigorous but sensual nature. On Jacob's name he denies that the phrase describes a grasp at all: twins are usually born an hour or more apart, and the words mean only that here there was no interval, a rare but recorded occurrence, the name signifying one who follows at another's heels, with the bad sense first put on it by Esau. Those who defend the literal reading from Hosea know only the English, he says, since the Hebrew there says he heeled his brother, that is, overreached him; and he objects that supplant is a poor rendering, containing a different metaphor. Of the word rendered plain he holds both that and perfect wrong, since it conveys no idea of blamelessness but only of general integrity and should everywhere be translated upright. Keil and Delitzsch have Esau wandering the fields and Jacob one whose disposition found pleasure in the quiet of home, sitting in the tents rather than merely dwelling in them.

schools.summary: Gill notes that boiling broth was no usual employment of Jacob's, passes on the Targum's tradition that this was the day Abraham died, lentils being the food of mourners, and adds that lentils were much used in Egypt and that those of Pelusium are named by Virgil and Martial. He lists what the birthright carried, honour and authority next to the parents, a double portion, the parental blessing, and above all the promises of the Messiah and the inheritance of Canaan as a type of the heavenly one, and supposes Rebekah knew from the oracle that these were designed for Jacob. Calvin attends to how Esau asks, the Hebrew running feed me with that red, that red, with the word pottage left out, the repetition and the omission showing the haste of a man whose eye was caught by the colour while hunger left him careless of consequences; he allows that in desiring food Esau does nothing worthy of reprehension, but the next words undo him, since to say what profit shall this birthright do to me betrays a profane desire wholly addicted to the earth. On the bargain he is harshest of all, calling it little different from the sport of children and asking what kind of bargain this was, since Jacob ought of his own accord to have satisfied his brother's hunger and, refusing, is open to the charge of inhumanity; his answer is that God was proving Esau's disposition in a small matter and bringing to light what lay hid in both.

Henry calls the birthright Esau's by providence but Jacob's by promise, a spiritual privilege carrying the excellency of dignity and of power as well as the double portion. On the buyer he is exactly balanced: Jacob is to be commended for coveting earnestly the best gifts, having grown acquainted with spiritual blessings in his tents while Esau lost the scent of them in the field, but he cannot be justified in taking advantage of a brother's necessity, nor was such an indirect course agreeable to his character as a plain man.

Clarke supplies a traveller's description from Barbary, where lentils dissolve easily into a mass and make a pottage of a chocolate colour, which he identifies with the red pottage of the story, and thinks the transaction shows Esau was so exhausted that he must have perished without immediate refreshment, having returned from the field too spent to make his own preparations. On what was sold he gives the usual list, then reports Calmet controverting most of it with apparent reason, holding the double portion the only incontestable right of the first-born and the rest conceded rather than fixed by law. Wesley reaches Calvin's verdict by another road, granting that if the birthright were only a temporal advantage there was something true in what Esau said, since worldly enjoyments stand us in no stead in a dying hour; but the thing being spiritual, his undervaluing of it was the greatest profaneness imaginable, and it is egregious folly to part with our interest in God and heaven for the riches of this world.

debates.question: Was Esau really in danger of death?

sides.position: yes — he was so exhausted he must have perished without immediate refreshment
the plea is beside the point — the words betray a profane mind addicted to the earth

schools.summary: Gill canvasses what Esau meant by being at the point to die, whether the common frailty of life, or, as Aben Ezra suggests, the danger he ran among wild beasts, and settles on his present faintness; he sees in the oath a precaution binding Esau to let his brother enjoy the birthright undisputed, observes that Jacob gave more than was bargained for, bread as well as pottage though nothing until the oath was taken, and sums the pair up by saying that, cunning as Esau was and plain as Jacob was, the plain man outwitted the cunning one. Calvin defends the demand, since Jacob took nothing from Esau but only sought confirmation of a right divinely granted him already, and did so with a pious intention, to establish the certainty of his own election. What he will not excuse is the seller, whose infatuation is that in the name and presence of God he does not hesitate to put his birthright to sale, making God himself a witness of his ingratitude. On the four flat verbs that close the chapter Calvin asks why so plain a sentence should be recorded and answers that it commends the piety of Jacob, who was no log of wood and, in preparing food, must have sharpened his own hunger, while on the other side the words describe Esau's indifference exactly.

Clarke will not have the buyer better than the seller. The apostle calls Esau profane, and rightly, since he should have perished rather than alienate such a right; but what, Clarke asks, of his most unnatural brother, who refused a starving man a morsel unless he gave up his birthright? Surely he who bought it in such circumstances was as bad as he who sold it, and by this act Jacob verified his claim to the name of supplanter. Wesley adds the aggravation on the other side: Esau used no means to get the bargain revoked and made no appeal to his father about it, so that what necessity might have excused his profaneness confirmed, and by his later neglect and contempt he put it past recall.

Ellicott reads the closing clause as graphic, there being no regret in it and no sad feeling that Esau had prolonged his life at too high a cost. He grants the meanness of the purchase and still finds a difference, since Jacob at least valued the privileges, and he traces the sequel as reward and punishment together: Jacob was confirmed in the birthright and became progenitor of the chosen race, yet from this day his life was full of danger and difficulty, fleeing his brother's enmity and falling perpetually victim to fraud and cruel deceit. Gradually his character ripened, until the scheming Jacob became an Israel, and in his pious old age we see a man full of trust and faith, unworldly and unselfish, purified of his early infirmities and strengthened by sorrow.
